title: Commander Focus: Cycling Lands, Prepared Channel, & Marwyn, the Preserver
content:
The two things I love most in Magic: The Gathering are attached at the hips: Taking the most game actions of anyone at the table, and activated abilities. I would much rather be the player doing one seemingly pointless behavior a dozen times than slamming a splashy spell, or oversized threat, because the doing is more important than the result, at its core. Matt Sperling put it best, in saying “The player who performs the most game actions wins the game, and that player is always me”, because even if all you’re doing is exiling one card at a time from a graveyard, or duplicating a pointless counter, there’s something else that synergizes with that fruitless tic to result in victory. I say this all because the Commander I’m talking about today is about as close as Wizards has gotten to being a parody of my predilections: Marwyn, the Preserver. At her core, she’s a Groundskeeper in the Command Zone, albeit more flexible in terms of the ability’s cost and its legal targets. Not only that, but in providing Hexproof to your Lands, she’s insurance against the occasional Strip Mine that crops up at high power. It should be noted that Marwyn being redundancy for Groundskeeper gives her an obvious role, as another buddy of Six with whom she can loop Lion’s Eye Diamond, but I intend to showcase that Marwyn can be even meaner than Six, if you’re willing to cast off a few moral scruples. Marwyn, like our last Focus’ subject Immortus, is a card that only gets better relative to the power level of your podmates. If the idea of a union between Six and Erinis, Gloom Stalker gets you excited, this new Marwyn is for you.

“Return target land card from your graveyard to your hand”

First, let’s get a lay of the land: Marwyn is a very reasonable 2 mana, affords your Lands Hexproof, and can pay {2} at any time to put a Land from your yard into your hand. That cost, unlike Groundskeeper, is 2 generic mana, which does give us substantial freedom in terms of its payment. Our goal is to, bare minimum, enter into the midgame with Marwyn capable of activating 4 times per turn cycle—that’s the floor. Luckily, there are a number of ways to ensure we have spare mana for this endeavor, with some cards we’ve spoken about at-length on Commander Focus making a triumphant return: Victory Chimes, Bender’s Waterskin, & Urban Burgeoning. Each of these causes a mana source to untap during our opponents’ Untap Step, and in the case of Urban Burgeoning, we can enchant any Land, meaning something like a Guildless Commons which taps for 2+ mana entirely pays for Marwyn. This can be doubly exploited via Heartstone (although watch out, as it’s reciprocal) to reduce the input cost of Marwyn’s ability to {1}, or via Burgeoning, which can (hand providing) also result in ~1 extra mana per turn via a Land being put onto the battlefield. Once the engine starts humming, we’ll be activating Marwyn far more than just 4x per turn cycle, but I wanted to demonstrate that goal was attainable across most of your games. Still, what Lands are worth getting back a dozen times per turn cycle, surely there’s nothing that readily exploitable which gets itself back into the graveyard at a moment’s notice? If you silently cursed the name Boseiju, Who Endures, you’ve got the right idea.

Yes, Boseiju, the Green staple that acts as a difficult-to-counter answer to problematic Artifacts, Enchantments, & Nonbasic Lands is itself a Land which discards to activate. With Marwyn onboard, it effectively reads as a {2}{G} ability to pop one of those three permanent types, and replace it with a Basic (or depending on how commonplace proxies are, surveil, shock, or OG duals). While this does bump up our opponents’ mana, as opposed to a similar repeated source of removal like Aura Shards, that too is something we can use to our advantage. As a reminder, Carpet of Flowers is a rather funny Magic card, and if a player at the table has Blue, Boseiju allows you to crack them open like a pinata to reveal plenty of Islands for its effect. While Boseiju is the Land we’re most keen on recurring repeatedly, it’s far from the only one. Tranquil Thicket, Slippery Karst, & Desert of the Indomitable all allow you to go card-positive, and while they’re a bit expensive to get going in the midgame, once you’ve generated infinite mana with the LED combo having any of these available allows you to draw through your Library, and find the capstone to your win. To do so, you need to tutor one Creature, in Six, and a 0-mana Artifact, which brings us to the next touchpoint: Utility Lands. Not every Land we’re playing just wants to be discarded, as there’s more than one way to get a Land into the yard, with many of our strongest tools instead being self-sacrifice effects.

Start Trying to Make Fetch Happen

Every mother has their favorite, you know.

I would contend that, in the grand scheme of Magic’s canon of design, fetchlands are one of the most egregious mistakes. In any format with access to both fetches and any sort of dual or triome, their very existence hews away at the limitations of color identity, and the opportunity cost to splash; that’s less of an issue here, in a Monogreen deck, but I say this instead to highlight their power. Fetches are the reason Marwyn’s ability is never dead, and why we’re able to so aggressively churn through Lands in hand for a card like Ayula’s Influence. Being in Monogreen, we get access to 4 traditional untapped fetches, but we’re less excited about playing tap-fetches like Evolving Wilds. That is, however, with the exception of Hobbit Hole, appropriately appearing in The Hobbit. This is not only a slow-fetch, but also has the capacity to ditch itself to tutor a small suite of Creatures, with our lineup being Delighted Halfling as a standard mana dork, and Erinis, Gloom Stalker as a great blocker that can get back cards like Hobbit Hole directly to the battlefield. This also works wonders for recurring pieces like Lazotep Quarry, which can translate into one of a few very important Creatures, and Inventors’ Fair/Urza’s Saga, each of which serves as limited tutors for things Green otherwise can’t find. Heck, even multiple uses of Urza’s Cave can help us find crucial Lands, albeit at a pricy rate. One final card worth talking about in the context of the hole is Formless Genesis, technically a Hobbit Kindred card, which is a phenomenal way to make use of all the Lands Marwyn recurs; if you need blockers or pressure, it’s extremely accessible during the midgame. It’s worth noting that, in pursuit of a budget version of Marwyn, you can definitely fill some space in your manabase with more slow-fetches and have a pretty good time. For as strong as proper fetchlands are, the real meat of her ability is getting back Boseiju/cycling Lands, and swapping them between the hand and yard as often as possible.

With all of these means of doing the proverbial hokey pokey with our Lands, what’s the reward for shaking it all about? A lot of the best payoffs for gravebreak—the official term for ‘leaves the graveyard’ synergy—either don’t count Lands, or aren’t in Monogreen. What we do have remaining are things like Turntimber Sower (the best of these), and lifegain payoffs like Titania, Voice of Gaea & Skola Grovedancer. There’s also Dredger’s Insight, but that only triggers for lifegain when we recur Dryad Arbor. These payoffs don’t seem impressive, at least not on the surface, but can result in a solid amount of sustain in a deck that intends to play for the long game. In addition, there’s one other reason we intend to have a high life total, and that’s to spend it as a resource; those familiar with my work are likely aware that Harold and Bob, First Numens is my favorite Green deck of all time, and the idea of incorporating the Black idea of ‘life as a resource’ in Green is top of mind, for me. We aren’t doing that with Rad counters here, no, but instead with another synergy package which has been waiting for a home in the colors that finally comes to roost in Marwyn: Yavimaya Bloomsage, and the capacity for a Prepared Channel.

Be Prepared

Man, Ajani sure looks weird in this reality.

Channel’s legality is a thing of beauty, because outside of a fake formal like Brawl (sorry, Arena fans) it’s only available in a Restricted capacity. It’s iconic (see Channel Fireball), powerful, and unavailable—perfect reasons for Wizards to have reprinted it via a Prepare Creature in Secrets of Strixhaven Commander. The Bloomsage is a very safe design, in that it Prepares a Sorcery in the end step, meaning in theory you need to wait a turn rotation before having access to arguably the most powerful Green spell of all time. Of course, traditionally you even need to have a Creature with high enough power to get there, but with a payoff as powerful as this, circumvention is the name of the game; arriving in SOS were Biblioplex Tomekeeper & Skycoach Waypoint, which each cheat the Prepare timing for a functional cost of {4}, if you consider tapping a Land for an effect beyond mana as {1}. This got more redundant in Reality Fracture, with Hexhaven Dueling Arena, but what’s really prompted this package’s inclusion is Marwyn herself, and Carnivorous Cultivator. Between the two, and one of the Prepare Lands, we can chain tutors to get all the Lands we need to pop off.

With Cultivator being an autoinclude, and Bloomsage being a phenomenal way to get an arbitrary amount of Colorless mana for Marwyn activations, it came time to look for other Prepare options worth adding, given we were priced-in for mechanical synergy at this point. As a brief explanation for what I mean by that, in a deck like Marwyn that both asks for a substantial Basic Land inclusion (for fetches, etc) and fetches and Cycling Lands, the number of slots we have for utility Lands which don’t meet those criteria is slim. The opportunity cost to include cards like these which are—barring their combo with Prepare bodies—vanilla Colorless Lands is reasonably high. The other two Prepare Creatures which made it in are Emeritus of Abundance & Vastlands Scavenger, although you could make a case for a couple more, especially in a budget version. These are somewhat mirrors of one another, where Emeritus of Abundance re-Prepares easily and has a cheap way to get nonlands back from the yard, Scavenger is in theory a one-time effect which is reasonably expensive. The latter is far more appealing to re-Prepare, and in fact can even hit our Tomekeeper with its ability, an absolutely adorable interaction that’s come up in testing as part of a mill engine. Even so, though, it’s not a bad thing to get 2+ Regrowths in a single turn with the Emeritus, or turn on her Spell with a board state not conducive to attacking with a 3/4. Bloomsage aside, the Prepare bodies we’re playing are independently powerful cards which just get a slight boost by being re-Prepared, which causes the inclusion of cards like Tomekeeper and the Lands to sting less. Last note on this package: Emergence Zone is an honorary Prepare Land, as if we can hit the power threshold for Bloomsage naturally, her associated Channel can be cast at Flash speed if we’ve popped the Zone. This does mean we need to do the whole combo in our end step, but given we have Flash access and no timing restriction on Marwyn’s ability that’s not too difficult.

Marwynning

Lucky for Doof, there's only one legal non-Changeling Platypus in Commander.

I established fairly early on that Marwyn is essentially just a Legendary version of Groundskeeper in the well-known Six/LED combo, with the added bonus that all your extra mana can be funneled into getting back nonbasic Lands, some of which have cycling, which in turn draws your Library. This is all fairly straightforward, but what are we actually attempting to do? Short answer: Gain infinite life via one of a few lines we’ll talk about, then use Grinding Station and infinitely-recurred Artifacts to mill our opponents out. It’s not as clean as actually killing opponents, as there can be Instant-speed attempts to fight back during upkeep, but for this list it requires the fewest cards you don’t really want to draw. Let’s talk lifegain though, because infinite life in this deck actually can mean the end of the game, unlike in so many; this comes down to Yavimaya Bloomsage being a card we intend to break, and of course Marwyn being a Colorless outlet which can sorta draw. Any of our cards which gain life when a Land shifts around works, or with Dredger’s Insight, solely Arbor Elf. This can be paired with one of a few means of ‘dribbling the ball’, with Ayula’s Influence & Ashnod’s Altar being the easiest. A similar interaction exists with one of my favorite cards of all time, Cryptic Trilobite, and Invigorating Boon, which approaches infinite when paired with some other cost reducer for abilities. Do note that Prepared Spells aren’t abilities, but Cycling is, so Trilobite can pay for Marwyn’s activation and get back ~{C}{C} once per cycle, which goes fully infinite with a card like Fluctuator. On the topic of Fluctuator, it’s obviously pretty crazy here as a means of churning through our Cycling Lands with a cost of {2}, but honestly still feels great when turning your Desert of the Indomitable into a Tranquil Thicket.

Back to win conditions that don’t require a bunch of things to go right, however, and we have Magus of the Candelabra & Maze of Ith; each are phenomenal cards in their own right, but because Maze doesn’t remove the targeted Creature from combat, it can be paired with the Magus and Lands which tap for 2+ more mana than their targeted number (to account for Maze and going +1 on mana) in order to make infinite mana and Land untaps in the declare blockers step. As above, the fact that Marwyn is totally fine with doing her thing at Instant-speed is a huge boon here. If you’re looking to win right then and there, you can certainly play Swell of Growth for Emergence Zone (the only Monogreen means of putting a Land from hand onto the board at Instant-speed while drawing through our deck, I wish I was kidding). Part of the reason I adore building Monocolor is dredging the absolute dregs of Scryfall to find hyperspecific effects like this; with only one color to contend with, oddballs like Swell take the place of what would be more ‘normal’ pieces like Growth Spiral if we had access to Blue.

Example Decklist: No No, the Other Marwyn

Marwyn is a deeply weird Commander to build around because a lot of what she wants isn’t especially available in Green, unless you contort your mind to believe it so. Take for example the fact that we’re on a pretty minimal amount of ramp; Marwyn isn’t looking to go super wide super quickly, and instead aims to grind out value over time. As such, 3 mana rocks like Bender’s Waterskin end up providing substantially greater value than say, Cultivate, over the course of a game. Monument to Endurance is perhaps better here than any other Monogreen deck, doubly so given we can flex the Treasures it produces as fodder for Grinding Station. Emrakul, the Exigent Doom gives us an extra Land which taps for {C}{C} (helping us hit the threshold for Magus of the Candelabra), but that ramp also works at Instant-speed for all of our means of making mana during opponents’ turns, or even via sources like Thran Turbine. Note also that, if you want to insulate your combos, you can always Natural Order or the like into Ashaya, Soul of the Wild, who allows you to spread Marwyn’s Hexproof to your nontoken Creatures. This list is weird, and all the little considerations surrounding its peculiar internal synergy, from Cycling to Prepare, coalesces into something the color just hasn’t seen before. It has shades of my Harold and Bob list (which as mentioned is one of my favorite decks of all time), but its entire flow resembles far more a mid-Bracket 3 list co-opting the fringe cEDH Six list’s tools.

Decklists are kept updated, and may change with set releases.

This list is Bracket 3, and almost has to be, if you intend to get the most out of Marwyn. Her role as a Legendary Groundskeeper is part of the reason to put the card in the Command Zone, and the combo that effect has with Six and LED is cEDH playable. As such, if you lack Game Changers (or the ownership of/capacity to proxy LED), it’s far tougher to justify this Commander. At Bracket 2, you’re far more likely to reverse-engineer Monogreen Cycling, playing Shefet Monitor and similar to fully lean into that gameplan; the issue is that Cycling’s never really been a Green mechanic proper, unlike the Jeskai colors, so it lacks compelling payoffs beyond what we’re already playing. I’m not kidding when I say Invigorating Boon and Cryptic Trilobite is like the only neat thing Monogreen Cycling has going for it. Two of our three GC slots are spoken-for, in LED & Seedborn Muse, and the third comes down to your moral scruples, or lack thereof. You could choose to play Natural Order, and chuck a Muse or Ashaya onto the table early...or you could play an untouchable The Tabernacle at Pendrell Vale, and tax Creatures with no recourse. If you did want to do that, be sure to play Urborg/Petrified Hamlet as well, so it still taps for mana. Maybe find some new friends, too. On that note, the question emerges as to whether this can be pushed to Bracket 4, and that gets into discussions around whether Marwyn or Six is better in the Command Zone. I want to stress that Marwyn’s printing has improved Six’s viability demonstrably, but if you’re really getting down to brass tacks, the fact she has a redundant piece in Groundskeeper means Six is our limiting reagent for this little reaction, and as such belongs in the CZ. Marwyn’s an absolute blast...at Bracket 3.

Arboretum for Breakfast

Quintin Gleim manages to make Marwyn feel small amidst the roots, an antithesis to her destructive Echoverse counterpart.

I was going to start this conclusion with a witticism about the peculiar nature of a Cycling+Prepare deck in Monogreen, but I can’t hide my excitement about finding a home for the Bloomsage line. I’ve mentioned that option as something Green can do since the card was initially spoiled, and I’ve been waiting for a Commander in the color(s) with a compelling Colorless mana outlet in the months since Secrets of Strixhaven. Well, she’s here, and her name is Marwyn. The other Marwyn, as my list’s name alludes to, because this is a character with a shocking pedigree in terms of Legendary Creatures; the original Marwyn, the Nurturer is one of the best Elfball Commanders of all time, and in her day saw pretty extensive play in cEDH as the fastest means of comboing off with Wirewood Symbiote. This Marwyn takes things quite a bit more slowly, and thankfully for me doesn’t require a typal gameplan (unless you count Halflingcycling). What does tie everything together though is a pursued sensation, a feeling: You get to drive stick in a format dominated by automatic.

It’s rarely the more efficient option to drive a manual car these days, as outside of high-performance vehicles it’s been slowly phased-out of most models. The thing is though, manual uses all four limbs, it keeps you active, it keeps you awake. Much like Marwyn, or any Commander whose gameplan is about doing small adjustments to card zones and liquid advantage every turn, four turns per cycle, stick keeps you engaged. A lot of the worst habits that arise from Commander do so because players intend to perform their linear gameplan, pass the turn, and enter torpor until the time comes round for them to act once more. If you aren’t thinking about what Land to pull back, what abilities you can flex, etc you can lapse in consciousness and tune out when it isn’t your turn, and uninteractive games like that tend to be dull experiences for all involved; I’m not saying this particular Marwyn list is interaction-dense, but rather that it calls upon you, the human sitting at the table, to interact and handle timings and game actions during other players’ turns. Your strandbeest of mediocre Cycling Lands and repeated Boseijus scurrying across the sands is one propelled by the winds of the turn cycle. If you didn’t have three opponents, you’d do half as much. All that’s to say, I wholly recommend Marwyn, and the only reason she’s not entering my paper lists comes down to my heart being claimed by a different peculiar, Land-oriented Monogreen Commander that paradoxically plays no Landfall. Two nickels, etc etc.

Until next time, Marwyn doesn’t care a whit, Marwyn doesn’t share our devotion to...style.

title: TheChirurgeon's Road Through 2026, Part 42: The Las Vegas Open
content:
Welcome back, Dear Reader, to my ongoing blog of hobby and competitive play progress through 2026. Last week I talked about the point drops and how they affect Death Guard, and I tested out a new list that focused on making the most of said drops, bringing an assload of beefy, fast units to the table to overwhelm opponents. I'm still mulling over that list, but I've been traveling for the past week, including a trip to the 2026 Las Vegas Open... which included no games. But there's still plenty to talk about, so let's dig in.

Why Did I go to LVO?

This is ironically the third time I've been to the Las Vegas Open's main event - I went to the Teams Tournament back in January and plan to go again - but also the third time I've gone without actually playing in the event. Each of the last two times I attended, it was to play secret preview games of Spearhead and 40k tenth edition, respectively. So LVO is always a weird experience for me, a convention where I'm attending but not playing and also it's the biggest 40k tournament in the country.

What I'm typically there to do - besides playing secret games - is business development for Tabletop Battles. I'm there to shake babies and kiss hands, or something like that. I'll meet up with the amazing staff at Frontline Gaming (shout out to Jake, who's always fun to hang out with), but I'll also use it as an opportunity to talk to the other companies at the event, connect on what they're doing, and talk about how we can collaborate.

Case in point: the Tabletop Titans have a new game called Wyldwood coming out that they just put out a Kickstarter for. We've been working with them on it, and may do more coverage in the future, but while I was at the event I took the opportunity to stop by their booth and talk to Adrian Phillips about the game, how it was doing, and what we might do together in the future. Sponsored content on Tabletop Battles is always an interesting process; we do not charge for reviews (and have sent back review copies when we felt games were bad), and outside of Kickstarter announcements the content we charge for tends to be the kinds of things we'd publish anyways - a tactics guide on a faction or paint tutorials. Our big ask on these is that the publisher cover the cost of writing the article for our authors. But the goal is that these end up being helpful resources with good SEO - an informative article on how to play a faction written by people who've tested and liked your game is a great resource for players.

So a lot of the work I'm doing at LVO when I'm there is stuff like that. This year, a big part of that was Bandai Namco's new game, Gundam Assemble, which features the mobile suits waging battle on a hex map with cards and dice. I played the upsized version of the game in a demo to get a feel for it, and I enjoyed it. I need to see how list building and deck construction works in the game before I make a final decision on it but I picked up a starter kit for it because it was only $35 (insane value) and it came with Gundam Wing models. Easy sell.

The other reason I was at LVO was to help Norman run the Sunday StarCraft tournament we'd signed up to run. We've been doing a lot of work to bring StarCraft support to the Tabletop Battles App, and we're also really interested in running tournaments for the game. It's got a wonderful, tight ruleset that lends itself well to competitive play at the tournament level. I'm not here to actually help Norman run the event so much as just be around while he does, so he won't be bored. Which is great, because Norman and I can talk about anything, forever - see our Patreon-only Podcast - and in a similar fashion to Greg, he and I can just sit around making each other laugh for hours.

Friday night we decided to grab dinner together as my wife, Mrs. Niche Tea, was out grabbing dinner with her parents and our schedules just weren't lined up. On the recommendation of a friend, we went to a steakhouse off the strip called Primal. It's got medieval theming - think suits of armor and wax candles - and some solid selections. It also had these fucked-up angled water glasses that made me feel like I was losing my mind whenever I looked at them:

Norman and I ended up splitting a 32oz ribeye Steak and each getting a baked potato - these were ridiculous 1-pound monsters, plus some mushrooms and brussels sprouts to ensure we weren't just eating meat and potatoes. The steak itself was excellent and the potato was solid. We left Primal properly sated, heading back over to the venue for a bit before calling it a night. I didn't take a picture of the steak before we ate it, so enjoy this photo of the bone from the thing:

I met up with Mrs. Niche Tea back at our hotel shortly after dinner and made our way back to the hotel room to settle down. She was unfortunately not feeling well the entire weekend, which freed me up to do more LVO stuff but also meant she was struggling through our group activities. I was doing fine.

Well, kind of. I woke up to go to the bathroom at 3am.

And again at 4am.

And 5am.

And 6am.

And seven. I was starting to suspect I had contracted whatever my wife had and she had more than just traveler's sickness but then I opened up Discord to coordinate with Norman and it turns out he was feeling it too:

And like, I wasn't happy Norman was shitting constantly, but at the same time I also was a bit relieved we could immediately pinpoint the cause. Makes it way easier to weather that storm if I know I can just eat a banana and down some Immodium and try and get through the day. it was... challenging, though the Immodium did its job for me pretty well through the afternoon and I ended up stabilizing, especially after eating a lot of rice at dinner.

The big challenge we faced on Saturday was terrain: Thanks to an honest mix-up between us and FLG, we had no terrain for the StarCraft event. So we had to scramble a bit - we borrowed some sets from our players for some of the tables, and I bought every starter kit FLG had at their store to hastily assemble. Shout-out to The Army Painter for lending us some clippers to get it all clipped off the sprues.

We made good time with the process, getting three starter boxes clipped and assembled in about an hour, and using FLG's leftover 40k ruins and Halo terrain to build the other tables. All total, we had three full tables of StarCraft terrain and three that worked well enough using other terrain kits. Scrambling to get things done at the last minute isn't my favorite way to do things, but it's also something I kind of enjoy - that kind of hectic energy motivates me and gave us purpose and the stress was relatively minor.

We'd originally planed to go to Area 15 and visit Omega Mart - Meow Wolf's Vegas installation - around 2, but thanks to our detour in terrain sourcing and building, we showed up two hours later, giving us only about an hour and a half or so to wander through the place. It was really cool, and I'd like to go back at some point and spend real time in there and do more with the story.

The reason we didn't have much time was because we had a room to escape - on the recommendation of fellow Tabletop Battles author and escape room reviewer Theresa Wagner, we did the Blair Witch Escape room off the strip. It's definitely one of the most involved rooms I've done, with multiple rooms and live actors, and there were some legitimate jump scares in the thing. Which is not great when you are afraid of shitting your pants at any moment because the steak you at last night has been wreaking havoc on your innards all day.

The good news is that we made it out of the thing under time and with our crew - Me, the missus, Norman, RagnarokAngel, and "Contemptor" Kevin Stillman - with time to spare. We parted ways after that, as I had to head over to the exclusive Gundam Assemble content creator event, which was back at Area 15.

I wrote about this already this week, but the event itself was a cool hangout, with free drinks, demo tables paint tables, and previews of upcoming sets. We got some cool swag and took photos, grabbed drinks and passed on the snacks, and I sat down and talked to Travis cheng (HappyRaccoon) and John Rees (Can You Roll a Crit?) about the game for a while as Travis played through a game against his friend, taking the opportunity to actually stretch and play tactically. The demo games Bandai Namco had set up were fine, but they're geared more toward beginners and people who don't play wargames. I wanted to dig into the mechanics more and really play with the cards and the respawn mechanics.

The lighter load made sense for the event in that it seemed like a 70/30 mix of gundam/anime influencers vs. tabletop/wargames people while I was there. You could kind of tell who played lots of games because the mechanics are simple enough it took about five minutes to "get it" - the hardest part of the game to me is line of sight mechanics with hexes but I also figure those will take one game to iron out and internalize. Mrs. Niche Tea and I stayed at the event for about an hour, then went back to our hotel.

Sunday was a mix of two things: StarCraft (run by Norman) and the final day of the 40k singles event. I was personally rooting for fellow Tabletop Battles writer Innes Wilson in the event, and he had a stellar run with his Adeptus Mechanicus army, taking them all the way to the finals before eventually falling to Kit Smith Hanna. At one point Norman and I stopped by Innes' table during the semi-finals to check on his game against Jack Murphy and although we tried to stay out of the camera shot it turned out we were very much in the shot, leading to Andrew sending us this screenshot.

It's my favorite shot of the event, because it has such perfect "hanging out and chilling next to the table" energy. You can practically hear us going "fuck 'em up" Innes. At this point Innes was firmly in the driver's seat, having put a beacon unit of chicken walkers on Jack's home objective. Innes is always fun to talk to and hang out with, and I was sad to see him go down in the finals, though there's no shame in losing to Kit.

Sunday night we did all you can eat Korean BBQ with Alice and Kevin and called it a night shortly after. Our flight back was Monday morning and Mrs. Niche Tea was still dealing with her own stuff, though I'd more or less recovered by Monday morning and was eating fine. Norman and I once again ate way too much, but this time no one paid the price for it the next day - at least not to my knowledge, anyways.

The big takeaway this weekend? I want to play at Worlds. I kind of felt the itch being around 40k without playing in it all weekend, and I decided that if I'm going to the WCW in December, I'm going to play. So it's time to gear up for that.

Final Thoughts

That's it for this week. I've been in New York all week on other business but I'll be back with more games and hobby progress next week, making headway on my Emperor's Children and planning for the final quarter of the year and building my plan to take on the World Championships.

See you Thursday.

title: Has Magic: The Gathering abandoned Pioneer?
content:
For a long time, Pioneer has been the black sheep of Magic: The Gathering's format family. Pioneer players are very upset about the lack of attention Wizards gives them and fans have been declaring the death of the format since late 2024. So what's going on? Did Wizards of the Coast abandon its youngest child?

Still the newest Constructed format created for the game, Pioneer was introduced in that naively optimistic year, 2019, as a way to bridge the gap between Modern and Standard. Basically, the Modern card pool had gotten too large, and it no longer quite served the it was first supposed to have: a place for players to use their cards after they rotated out.

Pioneer would solve that problem, and for a while its wider cardpool gave players a higher-powered way to play that didn't reach the ridiculously optimized highs of Modern. It gave rise to plenty of exciting new decks and strategies that weren't seen anywhere else: decks like Greasefang, Rakdos Vampires, and Green Devotion.

Then one day, without warning, Wizards appears to have kicked Pioneer to the curb. It was left out of the competitive play schedule for two years straight. In 2025 and 2026 there haven't been any Pioneer Pro Tours or RCQs - no competitive Pioneer play at all, in fact, since 2024.

There aren't many worse ways you could harm a constructed format than cutting its competitive scene. Sure, Pioneer might be able to bubble along okay as a 'kitchen table' format, and most players aren't trying to go to tournaments. But competitive play fuels interest in the format and keeps it healthy in ways that aren't always instantly apparent.

If Pioneer has top-level tournaments, this incentivizes the best Magic players in the business to pore over the format and find the strongest builds, the most exciting brews, and new tools for countering decks that seem unstoppable. Without that incentive, the evolving metagame, with decks rising and falling in response to one another, stagnates. The top decks stick around for longer, and with less good data, it's less obvious to Wizards when they need to step in and make bans.

That's evidenced by the fact there have only been two Pioneer bans since 2024, and they've basically followed Standard's lead, taking out the utterly broken cards that were also banned from the rotating format. Recently a ban article said "It's been a quiet period for Pioneer". There's a good reason for that!

While there's an argument that a lack of tournament play might mean freer gameplay, where less optimal builds aren't squeezed out, it doesn't really work that way in practice. After all, fans can always choose to play a more casual game, but unless you're one of these highly skilled players who can effortlessly analyze a format, you can't make your home Pioneer game more competitive if there's no competitive scene.

Why has Wizards left Pioneer out in the cold? Well, there's not been any clear communication on that front. Some have argued that it's to make Standard more important now that UB sets are Standard-legal, but it might equally be a consequence of Standard becoming increasingly swollen in size.

With 6 or 7 Standard-legal sets a year and a three year rotation, a bloated Standard has become more equivalent to Pioneer from a power-level, play experience POV. You arguably don't need a place for the strongest rotated Standard cards when those cards don't rotate for years, and only the strongest see competitive play anyway.

In fact, the recent Pioneer meta has long resembled a slightly higher powered version of Standard, or Standard as it was before the latest round of banning. The best Pioneer decks of 2024 are still around, and going nowhere while there's no incentive to put them to the test, but above them we now have a Golgari deck powered by Badgermole Cub, Izzet Prowess, and Mono Red. Yikes.

There is a glimmering of hope, however. Back in May of this year it was tentatively confirmed that some level of competitive Pioneer play is back on the table for 2027, and that Wizards is looking for more ways to get players engaged with Pioneer on Arena as well. On the other hand, in August we got the Pro Tour dates and the events are Modern, Standard, Standard, and Standard.

A half-hearted Pioneer revival is not much better than no competitive Pioneer at all. After being deserted for so long, interest is going to take time to recover, and players might not be keen to jump in if it seems likely Wizards will lose interest by 2028. If all we get are a couple of Spotlight Series events, it's honestly going to feel like Pioneer has been set up to fail. If they do the bear minimum, the response will be lackluster, and WotC can use that data as a reason to pull the plug forever.

Hopefully, that's not the plan. But what every Pioneer player would really appreciate right now is some clear communication from Wizards, and a dedication that it will keep the format going.

      • Make out with someone the same gender as you (if you're straight) or different gender (if you're gay or lesbian) - bisexuals get to pick.

Kinky dares (really not safe for public!)

These dares are for dedicated freaks - don't use them unless you already know that everyone playing is keen for this level of kinkiness, understands how to be safe, and is sober enough to do everything safely.

      • Quiet time! Until you're next asked truth or dare, you need to wear a gag - if the host doesn't have any special equipment, this could always be someone's underwear.
      • Punishment time - let another player spank you. Agree the number they'll count to, and a safe word for them to stop if they smack a bit too hard…
      • Let another player spit their drink into your mouth.
      • Smell another player's sweat.
      • Let another player step on you.
      • Let another player drip candle wax on your skin - be careful, you should only ever do this with candles that have a low melting temperature, and start with a long drop distance, otherwise there's a risk of burns. This is not something you can do safely with regular candles.
      • Hold another player's dick while they go pee (or let another player hold your dick while you pee, if you're a penis-possessor).
      • Let another player scratch a message onto your back with their nails.
      • Show the other players how you like to be touched.
      • Sit in a cake - then let the other players eat it off you.
      • Pretend to be another player's pet until they release you from their care - allow them to give you commands, tie a leash to you, and maybe even pet you…
      • Get on your knees, and don't get up until the player that gave you this dare says you can. Be sure to thank them once you stand up!
      • Let the other players attach springy clothes pegs to your soft bits. Bonus points if they tie them all together on a string that can be whipped off as a forfeit…
      • Pretend to be a horse, and allow another player to ride you around the room three times - they get to spank you to go faster.
      • Let a chocolate melt in your mouth, then kiss it another player's mouth.
      • Use both hands at once to 'massage' two different players…
      • Go down on another player
      • Pour massage oil over your body and let the other player(s) rub it in. (Set limits about where they can rub it - nobody wants to leave a sex party with a yeast infection).
      • Time to lose control - let another player work on you with hands or mouth, and give them the choice whether you get to finish.
      • With a blindfold on, let another player (or players) use you - can you guess who it is?

How to play Truth or Dare

Playing Truth or Dare is super easy, even if dealing with the potential embarrassment of a spicy truth or ridiculous dare can ramp up the tension fast! Here's how to get a game started:

      1. Get some friends together - ideally folks you know well, but not so well that you already know all their dirtiest secrets.
      2. Sit in a rough circle - so everyone knows whose turn is next.
      3. Start playing - each player, in turn, gets asked: Truth or Dare?
        1. If they pick Truth, either the group as a whole, or the player who went last, asks them one of our questions above, and they must answer honestly, or perform a forfeit.
        2. If they pick Dare, it's the same - but they must perform a Dare, or face a forfeit if they refuse to try.
      4. Play as long as everyone's having fun - there's no scoring or winning in Truth or dare; the game just keeps going until most players want to stop (maybe you're getting bored, or it's time to head to the club). The key thing is to wrap things up before anyone stops having fun.

Top tips for a successful Truth or Dare night

We're a bit old and boring these days, but we played more than our share of Truth or Dare in college, and as seasoned game analyzers, we've got some useful tips you should follow to have the best possible game:

      • Read the room - Truth or Dare is a game about making each other a bit uncomfortable, that's the fun of it - but there's a fine line between breaking down barriers with your friends, and making people mad, sad, or freaked out. Especially if you're the party host, be mindful of how good a time everyone's having, and wade in politely if you think it's necessary to keep the whole group having fun.
      • Consider the couples - Couples are great for Truths, as they know where all each other's bodies are buried, and can unearth the most entertaining stuff. But they can make things boring when it comes to spicy dares - where's the fun in forcing people to kiss someone that's already their partner? Consider using house rules to make sure couples don't lean on each other to avoid their duty to the game!
      • Set no-go areas if necessary - A game where everyone's expected to spill their deepest secrets, even embarrassing ones, can occasionally touch on topics or areas that are particularly sensitive for certain players, or could even bring up traumatic memories. As the host, if you're already aware of risks like that, think of a way to introduce a house rule that avoids it coming up, without 'outing' the person - there's no shame in having a banned topics list. It might sound over-cautious, but we've had some rough moments like this in the past, and everyone's there to have fun - so think about it.

That's all for now! If you made it through my juiciest Truth or Dare questions, you might also enjoy our world-leading guide to the best sex board games.

title: [Warmachine] Competitive Innovations in the Iron Kingdoms- September 2026
content:
Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our monthly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each month our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the month’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

As the weather cools outside the Warmachine meta has heated up to a boiling point! Compared to previous months the actual total number of games has taken a sharp nose dive leaving the actual stats to be a bit muddled but the competitive innovations are on point as new innovations emerge and finalize ahead of what many consider to be the biggest event of the year: WARMACHINE WTC. For some it was time to recede and grind dozens of games in preparation, for others it was a month of getting those last chances to sharpen their skills at a high competitive level to stay in peak condition ahead of the global showdown.

As we start, a quick review of the filters we use for the data pulled here. For this series, we are only looking at ranked tournament games and are excluding online only events.

September Stats

In September we saw 1112 games played at 60 events. The NOVA IGQ and UK Nationals were the highlights of the month and continued to show how a global perspective helps show differing meta trends.

Note- All of the Legacy factions currently unavailable as a part of Warmachine 3D are grouped together in the “Legacy Armies” section, due to their lower number of games played per faction and lack of widespread availability.

Games Played

Compared to August, the number of games played cratered to almost 1/3 as summer came to a close. Between waning weather, kids going back to school, and gearing up for WTC fewer events were played but the general higher quality of those events tell a pretty clear story. The 2025 summer hotness of Old Umbrey and the 2026 summer hotness of Fane of Nyrro dominated the numbers due to a combination of raw faction strength and people wanting to just play with either their finally fully painted toys and their new toys. Normally we would be ringing alarm bells for breaking the 10% danger threshold but when data shrinks to this degree, odd spikes are expected. Outside of those two outliers the numbers generally leveled out as people defaulted to what was familiar and comfortable as for most not traveling to Europe, the final major event of the year after this month is Lock and Load US.

Faction Winrates

Fane of Nyrro along with Wicked Harvest (formally Grymkin in our data) dominated the winrates and while the overall playrate wasn't a concern by itself, the correlation of both the highest playrate AND the highest winrate is absolutely a red flag for balance. As a result, players of both factions should be bracing for very pointed adjustments in January if they haven't already. While factions like Old Umbrey, Shadowflame Shard, Kithguard, and Dark operations operating in the normal high ~50% range, a quirk of less games sampled allow for the 2026 under dog Thornfall Alliance to rocket up to the staggering 57% winrate off of very few games played by excellent pilots. Similar wild shifts between factions is evident all over the data meaning theres little to gleam outside of the absolute extremes. Both house Kallys and Gravediggers stand out for having enough games to draw worth while conclusions. The original representatives of Dusk have found their way back to the light through a sequence of events where skillful players have managed to properly position answers to the current meta. Bandit on the flip side has successfully brought many players back to the Cygnaran trenchers by heavily simplifying in-game options, but players broadly haven't quite had the same time as the pre-80mm die-hards to position the ranged army into a meta that started the year heavily tuned into gunlines.

September Event Breakdown

Credit: Steamforged Games

With a reduction in games played comes a reduction in events covered. That being said its not as if those games are of lesser quality. Both the venerated NOVA Open and UK Nationals showcased some of the best and most cutting edge that Warmachine had to offer. For many these were the events of the year, a culmination of their work with their best factions. For others they were the final crucibles to hone and master themselves in leading to the clash of countries WTC.

IGQ at NOVA

https://www.longshanks.org/event/34176/

One of the biggest table top events of the year, the health of the NOVA Open is typically a leading indicator for the health of any miniatures game. The more the event allocates its precious space to a given game the more it shows there's a ravenous demand for that game. With more sponsors signing on to the Warmachine side in Centurion Tactics and Gearforged Hobbies, its clear to see other companies are taking notice of our rapidly regrowing hobby.

Two major heavyweights to the tournament scene duked it out at one of the last major US Events of the year and the final major proving ground before WTC (World Teams Championship). This was the final round a brutal gauntlet of games for both players as this finals was bisected by the NOVA schedule with the Teams event the previous day. So bare minimum this was game 9 for both of them over 3 back to back to back days of playing. Graciously they were both able to share their thoughts going into the matchup:

Akers: Knowing the matchup well, Mother was the objectively correct choice into the Classic Old Witch set up. The scenario and board did not impede the plan in any way but at best it was going to be a 50/50. Typically this showdown comes down to either leveraging the army to clear the house or clear the other scoring models. These are plans that heavily depend on the opponent. The main strength of Convergence is the flexibility in list building but also the unparalleled flexibility in play, allowing him to pivot and move his primary strategy turn over turn due to the new-to-this-year extended range of the induction mechanic and the "Free" nature of powering up the Vectors (Convergence's name for their warjacks).

CDemunn: Not being as familiar with the matchup on a physical practice level as Akers, the choice was still obvious. With the potential for Akers to drop Mother, heretic was simply not the correct drop. Good guns for shooting infantry just rips that list to shreds. He wasn't certain which list Akers would choose but the only truly horrendous result would be that Mother vs Heretic game and nothing about terrain or objective placement swayed his thinking in any way. It would all come down to Old Witch vs the Iron Mother.

Eeking it out after a failed assasination run by Akers, CDemunn proved definitively that he is a living legend of this game by winning back to back NOVA opens. Like many Grymkin players we have covered the past few months, the Old Witch was mono-listed throughout the event. Per our brief discussion there simply wasn't any perfect predators for Witch that necessitated Heretic’s use. A truly dominant showing for an exceptionally dominant player.

Second Place: (Akers - Convergence of Cyriss)

Proving beyond a shadow of a doubt that Convergence is an underrepresented powerhouse, Akers once again shined in this event. The latter half of this year has been a sharpening of his Iron Mother list and this event proved to everyone that he could also play Lucant, the conventional front runner for best Convergence Caster. The list pairing as-is represents the standard sword and shield. Iron Mother is an adaptive sword able to utilize her feat for drastically pumping up the MAT and RAT of her army to laser down certain targets, spells that extend range threat, ways to arc her spells though her cohorts, and personal Servitors that increase damage. Whatever way Akers wanted to scalpel threats he had tools for. Lucant on the other hand is an anti-gun WALL capable of stacking armor to oblivion and dish damage back. Constantly reviving and empowering models to create an endless horde of metal bodies to throw into the wood chipper and dominate the board. Definitely a combo worth eyeing for the rest of the year and into the future 2027 meta.

title: D&D monster expert tells us how design has changed in 5.5e - for better and worse
content:
Few people outside Wizards of the Coast know as much about D&D monsters as Keith Ammann. He created The Monsters Know What They're Doing, a blog full of combat advice in 2016, and its popularity spawned an entire series of books. Now a full-time author and ENNIE winner, Ammann has released a remaster of a book that borrowed its title from that original blog.

The Monsters Know What They're Doing: Remonstered updates Ammann's original advice for the 5.5e rules revision. It released in the US on October 6, with a UK launch planned later down the line. This update seemed like the perfect opportunity to pick Ammann's brain on the differences between the two editions, and how this has changed his approach to monstering.

I recommend reading The Monsters Know What They're Doing, if you haven't already. The original book was a big help in my early days of Dungeon Mastering. Understanding the why behind each monster action made me a better planner, but it also gave me a stronger framework for improv decisions.

Its core design philosophy remains the same in the Remonstered edition. Ammann tells me his approach could be called simulationist, but "what I do is not necessarily optimization".

"It's important to me to create a game world that feels like it could really exist, where everything has implications", he explains. "There are a lot of monsters where I think the optimal strategy is not the most appropriate strategy, because the monster might not be smart or wise enough to employ the optimal tactic."

"I want it to be as true to its own nature as possible, as expressed by the rules, because the rules are the natural laws of the universe", he adds. "It's all in the service of the story. How does this monster behave in the world to maximize its chances of getting what it wants - and surviving?" "To me, the mechanical stuff is a way of roleplaying monsters."

Ammann's philosophy hasn't changed much in the past decade, but D&D's certainly has. Ammann summarizes 5.5e's approach as more sensible, but less story-driven.

"Part of a move in the game, not just in monster design, is away from beginning with narrative and then figuring out how you're going to model that mechanically", he says. "It's a move towards starting with a mechanic you want to implement and then figuring out how you justify it narratively."

Case in point: changes to damage types. Monsters no longer deal magical and non-magical attacks; if D&D wants to communicate this, it now has the same monster deal force, necrotic, radiant, psychic, or so on. Ammann argues this makes less logical sense in-universe. "It's not that a monster is hitting you with magical force; it's hitting you with a big claw, and you are magically unable to withstand the damage."

"The same goes for monsters now never being resistant to bludgeoning, piercing, or slashing damage from normal weapons", he adds. "It told a good story - only a magic weapon can pierce this creature's hide." "The trouble was, if nobody brought a magic weapon, the battle would take twice as long." "Instead, they got rid of that and simply increased the hit points", he says. "From a gameplay point of view, it's probably beneficial, but it takes away a bit from the narrative."

For Ammann, the most egregious example actually belongs to a D&D class. "One that drives me up the wall is a Barbarian class feature called Primal Knowledge", he says.

"While your Rage is active, you can make Stealth checks with Strength. A screaming hunk of meat is not more stealthy than a non-screaming hunk of meat!" "I'm sure they introduced Primal Knowledge to satisfy Barbarian players who want to do more as a class", he says, "but Rage - the name means something, right? The original feature is a way of telling a story." "Now, the mechanic has moved front-and-center, and now we have to twist the narrative to explain what we mean."

This move away from narrative has been further emphasized by cuts to lore text in rulebooks. Ammann relied on this flavor text to shape his advice for running monsters, so it meant several changes in the Remonstered edition. However, he recognizes D&D "had a difficult needle to thread". "They clearly wanted to include more art, which meant less room for text", he says. "They also wanted to be less prescriptive about how DMs should run certain monsters."

"In my opinion, they went a little bit too far toward the other extreme", he adds, "because what you have now is flavor text so short that someone new might not have the first idea about how the monster should be played". "It now depends more heavily on DMs having cultural exposure to D&D monsters."

"But on the flip side, one of the problems with the old way is that DMs might not have felt comfortable deviating from what's in the book", he continues. "It's a balancing act, and nobody's going to get it perfect every time."

It'd be wrong to paint Ammann as a 5.5e naysayer, despite these critiques. There are many changes to monsters he argues in favor of. For example, "I think the change in how legendary actions are handled is a significant improvement".

"Instead of having some that cost two or three legendary actions - which is hard to track but also hard to talk about - you now have legendary actions that can only be used once between the monster's turns." "It's much more sensible, and it's much easier to remember if you've used it already."

Whether a change is good or ill, Ammann's monster advice must adapt to reflect it. Some monsters are virtually untouched, while others have had more significant makeovers. There's also plenty of brand-new monsters to advise on.

One familiar face with a new do is the Lich, whose spell list changed significantly for the 2025 Monster Manual. "The spell I recommended leading with in the original Monsters Know What They're Doing, the 2025 Lich doesn't even have - there's no Cloudkill in the new stat block", Ammann says. "Now I have to completely rethink how a Lich is going to begin a combat encounter - there are many examples like this."

"In some cases, the changes had effects that might not seem significant for everyone, but were very significant for me", he tells me. "For example, Kenku are no longer humanoids - they're monstrosities." "To me, that change in creature type comes with a change in what they're driven by."

"As humanoids, they might be a little tribal, a little clan-ish - they're interested in protecting their society", he explains. "But as monstrosities - particularly monstrosities with an attachment to the Shadowfell which was not there before - you now have something less concerned with social relations and more concerned with food and territory." "That link to the Shadowfell also means they're going to be more brutal and nihilistic."

There is one change all monsters have been subject to in Remonstered: tip boxes. "I wanted to make sure readers were getting something that'd make it worthwhile for them to go and pick up the book, even if they have the original already," Ammann says.

"There are four kinds of tips", he explains. "There's Modifications you might make to the monster to bring it more in line with what I believe its nature to be. There's 'We Make a Good Team', which is other creatures you can pair these monsters with."

"There's Prepare the Ground, which are recommendations for favorable terrain the monster can take advantage of in tactical and cinematic ways, and there's Shenanigans, which are funny stunts and loopholes I've found in stat blocks you can take advantage of for humor or shock value." I'm personally pretty keen to see what Shenangigans are on the table.

Want to talk more about Dungeons and Dragons? We're always keen to chat about games in the Wargamer Discord. If you need a quick rules refresher before diving in, check out our guide to DnD classes.
