title: Sought-after Warhammer 40k Magic the Gathering decks are finally getting reprinted
content:
Wizards of the Coast is reprinting the extremely popular Warhammer 40,000 Magic the Gathering Commander decks, IGN reports. The decks went on sale in 2022 and were a massive hit with fans of both games, and prices on the secondary market now reflect that, with foil Collector's Edition decks trading for around $700.

The four 100 card decks, designed for Magic's popular four-player Commander format, are generally regarded as an early high water mark in WotC's 'Universes Beyond' program to bring outside IP into the collectible card game. Each deck is themed around one of four Warhammer 40k factions - the Tyranids, Chaos, Necrons, and Imperium - and contains a mixture of classic Magic cards with brand new Warhammer 40k art, and some totally original cards.

Writing on Thursday, IGN reports that Wizards of the Coast has confirmed a small reprint of the decks will soon be available to distributors and stores. It's not yet clear whether the Collector's Editions of the decks, in which every card has a shiny foil treatment, will be reprinted, nor what the retail price will be. The decks originally sold for $59.99.

I've got the Tyranid deck, and it's a pretty solid little starter deck for Commander, and wouldn't take much tuning up to turn it into something pretty powerful - I've not bothered to upgrade mine because the idea of mixing in non-Warhammer 40k characters makes my eye twitch. I'm in the minority I'm sure. A lot of the demand for the decks comes from the cards' mechanics, not their flavor.

The cards in the decks are all legal in Magic's "eternal" formats, play modes that allow players to use almost any card ever printed. A few 40k cards have seen play at a competitive level. Marneus Calgar became the basis for a CEDH (competitive Commander) deck; The Triumph of St Katherine, Chaos Defiler, Canoptek Scarab Swarm, and Poxwalkers have all seen play in Legacy. Plenty of the unique cards are also useful in the non-competitive, but extremely popular, Commander format.

This kind of demand drives secondary market prices up. Wizards of the Coast periodically reprints old cards in new products, but sprinkling cards with Warhammer 40k licensed characters on them into unrelated MTG sets isn't really an option. The idea that WotC would just reprint the original decks wholesale is surprising because, well… it just doesn't do that, normally.

Did you grab the 40k commander decks when you had the chance? Are you planning to pick them up? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: These Pokémon skateboards are sold like cards, with random draws and chase rares
content:
Santa Cruz Skateboards is releasing a licensed range of skateboard decks that look like they've had a jumbo-sized Pokémon card slapped on the top. These boards, which launch October 17, 2026, are coming out in conjunction with the trading card game's 30th anniversary celebration, and as a result the maker has created 30 different designs.

They also seem to be sold quite like trading cards - for better or worse. They're in blind bags, which means you don't know what you're going to get when you pick one up. There are also three rarer 'chase skateboards' you can open (of course there are). These are an additional three designs, on top of the 30 regular versions, and they're easy to spot - they're covered in many different Pokémon cards. Right now we've no idea what the 'pull rates' will be, though, so who's to say how rare they'll be.

The 'Pokémon blind bag decks' feature card art from the Pokémon TCG. Like 30th Celebration's classic collection, these are all famous cards taken from the entire history of the TCG. These range from Base Set Blastoise, Charizard, and Venusaur to modern classics like Moonbreon. You'll find a number of the selected cards in our rare Pokémon cards guide.

Or perhaps it's more accurate to say the boards feature 'art of cards'. Instead of trying to make each Pokémon card's illustration fit the dimensions of a skateboard, the designers have simply added a depiction of the card to the board. The rest of the design is textured background art that matches the vibe of the card on the board.

No price has been revealed for these products just yet, but Santa Cruz Skateboard decks usually range from about $85 to $105. That's a lot of cash to put down on a randomized product, so perhaps there'll be some kind of discount to account for that random element. After all, it would suck to splash out and end up with a design you really hated.

While most of the cards chosen have a similar 'radical' vibe, there are a few cuter boards, like the Gardevoir or Sylveon. And - I hate to say it - I think one or two look kind of 'derpy', in particular that Jolteon and that Lucario.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Star Wars Legion Mandalorian Custom Characters
content:
Welcome back to the end of our Mandalorian unit reviews. Now that some time has passed and the Mandalorians have found their place in Legion it is time for us to go over the customizable characters and the custom clan rules, with some light touches on how to utilize your own custom Mandalorian leaders in the other clans as well. These are some of the most exciting models to come with the army release and it has been a joy to paint and play them on the tabletop, and with all that said let's get to the review.

What are Customizable Characters?

For those who are a bit newer, Star Wars Legion has a Commander and Operative for every army that is a customizable character with a plethora of upgrades available to them. These characters can be tailored towards your personal play style as well as coming with bits for you to customize their looks as well. These characters help players bring out their personal play styles in their lists, and the customizable Mandalorians keep this theme going.

Custom Mandalorian Leader

Unlike most custom commanders the Mandalorian Leader has multiple built in keywords. Jump 2 gives the unit the ability to make a move ignoring or landing on terrain of the same height. Impervious reduces the Pierce value of weapons it is defending against but 1, this can be to a minimum of 0 so it is essentially immune to Pierce 1 weapons. The final keyword on the units card is Retinue: Mandalorian Warriors which allows you to give the unit stated (in this case Mandalorian Warriors) 1 Aim or Dodge token. As a base this is already a fairly supportive commander unit before upgrades.

Equip is a keyword that forces you to take upgrades on a unit, for the Mandalorian Leader it needs to equip an Armament upgrade and a Doctrine upgrade. Doctrines are a unique upgrade for the custom characters that drastically change how the character functions, but enough about the unit card the real interesting part of the Mandalorian Commander comes from the upgrades unique to it.

These 2 Doctrines are able to be taken by both the Leader and Hunter. Battlemaster provides the unit the ability to use an expendable upgrade as an exhaustable upgrade instead the first time you use it. This can allow you to use a whipcord twice, or a flamethrower twice, rockets, and so on. The upgrade also adds the keyword Death From Above which removes the defending units cover when you attack them from terrain that is a higher elevation than your attack target. This makes the Mandalorian Leader a mobile attacker that can hunt units effectively across the battlefield. Deadeye is a Doctrine that gives the Unit Target 1 and Sharpshooter 1. Target gives the unit an Aim token if it is issued an order and Sharpshooter reduces cover of units defending from this units attacks. This is a generically strong combination of aggressive keywords that support any weapon on the model, short or long range. This does not improve the damage of melee weapons since in melee cover does not apply.

The Mandalorian Leader has a unique Doctrine only it can equip. War Party Leader gives the unit Direct: Mercenary Trooper, Inspire 1, and it increases the courage value of the unit by 1. This gives the Mandalorian Leader a courage bubble of 3 for a mostly courage 2 army which makes your units harder to panic in general. Direct lets this unit order a unit to the unit the Direct keyword is referencing, which in this case is any unit that is both a Mercenary and a Trooper. For instance with the upgrade Underworld Connections you can order any unit with any affiliation or if you use the Mandalorian Clan upgrade of your choice you can order units of those affiliations. Inspire 1 removes a suppression token from a unit at the end of the Mandalorian Leaders activation.

The armament upgrades are available to both units, there are 2 melee weapons and 3 ranged weapons. The Dual Armaments add the keyword Charge which lest the unit make a melee attack action when it moves into melee with a unit and Gunslinger which lets the unit make a ranged attack towards another unit in range after it makes a ranged attack. The Vibroknives have High Velocity which disable your opponents Dodge tokens when you attack them and Pierce 1 which cancels 1 successful defense roll. The 3 white dice and 3 black dice aren't the most damage but it does have some strong keywords. The EE-3 Carbine has Overwhelm which adds an extra suppression on the defending unit when you use an Aim token to re-roll dice. This along with the 1 red and 3 black dice pool combos well with Deadeye wince you will commonly have an Aim token. The GALAAR-15 Carbine is 4 black dice at range 1-3 which is boring with a lack of extra keywords but it is a free way to increase the units range. The GALAAR-90 Sniper Rifle adds Sharpshooter 1 (which can stack with Sharpshooter 1 to become Sharpshooter 2 and essentially negate heavy cover) and has the old sniper upgrades dicepool, High Velocity, and Pierce 1. It isn't a lot of damage but it can be a consistent way to push damage through to units. The Vibrosword provides the unit with Charge and Duelist, which is a complicated keyword but in essence gives Pierce 1 when you spend an Aim to re-roll dice and provides Immune: Pierce when you spend a Dodge both in melee. This can make the Vibrosword Pierce 2 if you spent an Aim and with the dicepool it can do a decent amount of damage to units while also being defensible in melee. The interesting part of the Vibrosword is that it allows you to use Shield tokens in melee which you normally are not able to do.

The Mandalorian Leader comes with 1 command card. Honor and Strength is a 3 pip that issues any 3 units a faceup order token. During this round as long as your Mandalorian Leader is not suppressed or panicked Mandalorian Troopers within range 2 upgrade 2 of their dice. In most cases this will bring black dice to red dice which can really increase the effectiveness of your Mandalorian Warriors or even other characters. This command card also downgrades enemy attack dice within range 1 of the Mandalorian Leader unit which can reduce the effectiveness of attack, especially if they already have Pierce which is reduced by the Mandalorian units Impervious.

Mandalorian Hunter

The Mandalorian hunter is the other half of the box. The Mandalorian Hunter comes with the same 2 keywords as the Leader but also comes with Mercenary: all factions which greatly increases the use cases for the unit, and adds something to the Republic that they do not have but we will get there when we get to the unique Doctrine for this unit. Unlike the Leader counterpart the Hunter does not have surge to defend which causes it to be a little easier to remove than the Leader but it is cheaper by a large margin to compensate for that.

The Hunter has access to Battlemaster and Deadeye and they add the same effectiveness to this unit like they do to the Commander. The Mandalorian Hunter being an Operative does make it easier to justify it not babysitting units and moving off on its own to deal with other characters on the battlefield. The Mandalorian Hunter does have a unique Doctrine.

Guild Member lets you create your own custom bounty hunter that can be used across all the factions. This is one of the most exciting parts of the Mandalorin Hunter, and provides the Republic with the bounty hunter they have never had. This also makes the Mandalorian Hunter more efficient and defensive at fighting its Bounty target (or any Bounty target for that matter) since it provides an Aim and a Dodge if you are fighting against your Bounty target. With all this said, what is Bounty? Bounty makes you choose an opponents Operative or Commander unit at the beginning of the game during setup and give it a Bounty token. This token cannot be removed by any normal means except if that Bounty target is defeated. If a Bounty a unit with the Bounty keyword defeats a unit with a Bounty token that Bounty token becomes 1 VP for the player controlling the unit with Bounty. Any unit with Bounty can claim the VP (Victory Point), they do not have to target specifically the unit they assigned the token to.

There is 1 other unique upgrade for the Mandalorian Hunter that puts it on par with its Mandalorian Leader counterpart, and that is Full Beskar Armor.

This provides the Mandalorian Hunter with surge to defend which makes the Mandalorian Hunter just as survivable as the Mandalorian Leader.

The 2 units share the same weapons, but the Mandalorian Hunter can utilize the Pierce weapons better since the Bounty Hunter keyword requires it to defeat its Bounty target to collect the VP. Melee is usually a preferable range for bounty hunters so they can be protected from being shot by other units. This makes the Vibrosword a fantastic choice for the Hunter.

The Mandalorian has 1 command card that is a 1 pip. No Escape only gives an order to the Mandalorian Hunter but it prevents units engaged with or being attacked by the Mandalorian Hunter from spending Dodge, Aim, or Surge tokens. This makes the already deadly Mandalorian Hunter that can be attacking with Pierce 2 even deadlier since it can prevent Surge tokens from being used as well.

Each of these units can be taken by the different Mandalorian Clans since they have the Mandalorian Clan upgrade slot. This lets you provide them with the different clan keywords which only add to the customizability of these characters. You can take a more aggressive Mandalorian Hunter with the Vibrosword and Victory or Death from the Clan Saxon upgrade so you can get free tokens or a defensive Mandalorian Leader with the Sniper, War Party Leader and We Fight for our Family so you can spread dodge tokens along with orders to other units. These units add a force multiplier to your army's and can be tailored for exactly what your army list needs.

Custom Mandalorian Clan

The Mandalorian Battleforce comes with a fifth clan that we have yet to talk about. The Custom Clan is unique from the other clans because you get a choice of 2 special rules from a list of 6.

In order to get this benefit you lock yourself out of all of the named characters and all veteran units as well. You also cannot bring any clan upgrades on your other units so you are locked out of all the clan upgrades. Between the 6 options some of the more interesting ones are Guns for Hire which let you bring a vehicle into your list, which the most interesting seems to be the AA-5 Speeder Truck because it can transport units and has more open upgrade slots. Another interesting option is Rapid Deployment which lets you set aside 2 units to be deployed onto the board not only in your deployment zone like Infiltrate, but anywhere range 2 away from all enemy units. This can be fun to combine with other options such as Guns for Hire so you can deploy your transport anywhere on the board and deliver a unit of Mandalorian Warriors behind the deploying vehicle. There are so many options available within these 6 choices for you to tailor a list completely for yourself and play Star Wars Legion uniquely from other players. You will need to decide if giving up the other clans is worth it for you but that is the fun part of list building in general is choosing which options work better for your personal style of play.

Sleuth's Mandalorian Leader

  • War Party Leader
  • Stuck in
  • GALAAR-90 Sniper Rifle
  • Clan Wren
Credit: Mandalorian Sleuth

With that all of the options for your Mandalorian armies have been covered, so tell us how do you enjoy playing your Mandalorians? Do you enjoy taking a custom clan, or do you enjoy mixing up all your options for a soup list that exemplifies your favorite styles of play? I personally enjoy my pure clan Wren list that brings a custom Mandalorian Leader designed to alleviate the suppression issues that Guardian 1 army wide can have.

Sorry for running a tad late this week folks. I was at the Las Vegas Open myself this weekend so it was a bit of a long trip getting back and I am exhausted.

So this week, as expected, we will cover the Las Vegas Open, one of the biggest events of the year. We also have the similarly sized Sydney Grand Tournament down in Australia, and right next door is the Auckland AOS GT in New Zealand.

A pretty novel list, using a shielded Vizzik to force fire away from the Nightrunners which do the bulk of the damage with multiple crit mortals, a pretty clever trick.

title: [Crisis Protocol] Competitive Innovations in the Danger Room, September 2026
content:
Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our monthly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each month our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the month’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

Greetings, True Believers!

We finally got the biggest update in all of the history of MCP with hundreds of characters getting changes to their health and some key affiliations getting major overhauls.

For these competitive innovation articles usually I continue on from where the last article stopped but this time we're only looking at results from events since the August update to take a look at how it has shaken up the meta. As a reminder of some of the changes in that update take a look at our article here. 

I've restricted the data to only include rated events with more than 15 people in case anyone wanted to look into more detail on Longshanks.

Affiliations by Winrate

Hellfire Club

Hellfire Club Credit - Alfred_Pharius

The Hellfire Club sit at the top of the competitive meta with a very healthy 63% win rate across 219 games.

Since her first update earlier in the year Emma Frost has become a dominant force and one of the premier 4 threat characters in the game. With even more health now, she is an anchor to the Hellfire Club and brings a toolbox of useful abilities as well as a strong leadership. On top of that, key characters like Omega Red and Mr Sinister received improvements to their output and mobility giving them a durable 12 threat core.

The Hellfire Club bring some tough characters on top of a leadership that heals them, if you don't manage to kill them quickly they can easily snowball out of control.

If you are struggling to beat the Hellfire club some potential counters could be characters like Ultron Metal Tyrant who has strong mystic defenses and can't be displaced by most of the Hellfire Club's tricks.

Wakanda

Erik Killmonger for Marvel Crisis Protocol MCP painted by Crab-stuffed Mushrooms

Wakanda are proving strong in this new world and despite the nerfs to King T'Challa they achieved a 62% win rate over 187 games.

Earlier in the year M'Baku was the preferred Wakanda leader but since the update Killmonger Usurper appears to have taken the throne from him. Usurper received some nice quality of life improvements gaining more health, better timing on his leadership and the ability to use his covert armaments attack in retaliation when he is attacked.

Wakanda have always been a strong affiliation and Wakanda forever remains one of the strongest cards in the game. The ability to suddenly make additional attacks with all of your affiliated characters can swing you from a losing position to a winning one very quickly.

New Mutants

credit: Brushwizard

The New Mutants are up next with a very respectable 58% win rate across 55 rated games. This one will need to come with a pinch of salt as the number of games is comparatively lower than the rest of the list but that doesn't mean we need to count them out.

The biggest change to the New Mutants post update was the addition of Honey Badger to the affiliation list. She gets a lot of benefit from Magik's Cry for Help leadership placing next to whichever ally is being attacked and taunting the attacker preventing them making any follow up attacks. She additionally gained the ability to pick up extracts meaning she can now contribute to the scenario as well as attrition.

X-23 and Honey Badger both being affiliated mean that any attack an opponent makes to either of them can lead to a huge amount of movement for the New Mutants player.

We've now seen what Mirage and her leadership might bring and although the leadership itself is underwhelming Mirage as a character seems strong.

The New Mutants do have one key weakness which prevents them ever being on top and that is that both of their leaderships require the opponent to interact with them. Though counterintuitive the best thing to do when facing the New Mutants is often to ignore them preventing them from gaining any leadership benefit.

SHIELD

The agents of SHIELD remained strong, winning 57% of their 151 recorded games.

During the previous competitive innovations period, SHIELD were at the top of the meta but some recent changes have brought them down a couple of rungs. The biggest change was the update to Baron Zemo's Strategic Genius rerolls. Previously people would take this alongside rerolls from Namor's Charismatic Leader ability to create a "Double Bubble" of stacking rerolls. Although this is still possible it isn't nearly as strong as it once was now that Zemo has to pay for his rerolls and that they are once per turn.

Despite these changes SHIELD still has some of the best tactics cards in the game such as Battlefield Medicine and The Shieldmobile. On top of that they have multiple ways to safely pick up and manipulate extracts and some excellent defensive abilities. With these things combined if SHIELD get ahead on points it can become very difficult to claw things back from them.

Web Warriors

Web Warriors. Credit: head58

The Web Warriors round out the top 5 with a 56% win rate across 323 games.

The Web Warriors had an interesting time with the latest update as many of their most popular characters had no changes while their underused characters all got better. We can see from which leaders were used that Miles Morales is now the least popular leader with the lowest win rate leadership which we never would have said last year.

The addition of the very strong character Ultimate Spider-Man may be another reason that the 3 threat Miles Morales has lost popularity as they share an alter ego and cannot be taken together.

Best of the Rest

A further nine affiliations sit just above the 50% win-rate mark.

The Convocation have a healthy 54% in rate across 171 games. The biggest update they received in August was the addition of the Scarlet Witch to the roster. She brings some much needed punch to the affiliation playing a similar role to Blue Marvel in the Defenders.

The Black Order also performed above average with a 52% win rate also helped by the addition of Nebula to their affiliation list. Corvus Glaive and Proxima Midnight have become a terror in the meta after their updates and the Black Order seem to have benefited from their changes compared to where they were earlier in the year.

The Midnight Sons, Guardians of the Galaxy and Mighty Avengers rounded out the top 10 affiliations in this period all with a healthy 52% win rate.

Final Thoughts

The August update has certainly shaken up the competitive scene with dominant affiliations such as the Servants of the Apocalypse no longer making the top 10. And underplayed affiliations like the Hellfire Club now creeping into the top tables. The best lists still aren't solved and there are some big events to come later in the year. It will be interesting to see how things shake up!

title: Dating app study claims tabletop gamers are 65% more likely to be polyamorous
content:
If you've spent much time on the tabletop gaming internet, you'll have seen memes about the overlap between polyamory and tabletop gaming - jokes that the real reason for non-monogamous relationships is neither sex, nor companionship, nor financial stability, it's a regular group of people you can play D&D and board games with. Adventurous dating app Feeld says it's got data to back up the memes - among its users, tabletop gamers are 65% more likely than non-gamers to be polyamorous or practice another form of ethical non-monogamy (ENM).

Feeld advertises itself as the dating app for non-traditional relationships. It doesn't exclude people looking for long-term, straight, monogamous relationships, but its marketing focuses on every other kind of connection you could try to make. It's an app for LGBTQ+ folks, kinksters, swingers, couples looking to meet a third, poly folks, people searching for ethically non-monogamous hookups and relationships, and so on. Combine that with all of a dating app's regular data about people's interests, and the analysts have found some interesting correlations.

According to a report by data analyst L Nichols published on Feeld's website on September 15, 33% of Feeld users practice ENM; for tabletop gamers (encompassing everything from running a Dungeons and Dragons group to playing the best board games), that figure rises to 52%. Tabletop gamers on Feeld are 65% more likely to practice ENM than non-tabletop gamers. Conversely, poly and ENM Feeld users are more than twice as likely to list 'tabletop games' as one of their interests, compared to monogamous app users.

Now you could infer from the data that something similar happens in the general population: while rates of ENM are lower in the general population than on Feeld, a similar proportional increase may exist among tabletop gamers. The article has a lot of fun theories pointing to similarities between ENM practice and tabletop gaming that might explain that overlap: an acute awareness of time management, appreciation for the importance of rules and boundaries, a diverse community that often include marginalized folks.

But I'm gonna be a real stats Grinch about this. The data shows that ENM tabletop gamers are more likely than ENM non-gamers to appear in this data set, and that may just mean that being a tabletop gamer is a very effective vector for ENM folks to learn about the app. It's a social hobby and a great vector for the spread of information; nerd media is also clustered around online micro-celebrities who talk about very different topics compared to the average magazine columnist or TV pundit.

While Feeld's article leads with the stats about tabletop gamers, that's not the only group it's got data for. Anime fans and cosplayers are apparently 38% more likely to practice ENM; comic readers are 50% more likely; the grouping of tabletop gamers and fantasy literature readers is 65% more likely; and sci-fi fans are a whopping 80% more likely. What happens at Trekcon doesn't necessarily stay at Trekcon, it seems.

My stats Grinch could keep grumbling about the lack of n values here - we don't know if the sample sizes are large enough for those data to be statistically significant. Despite how much the report resembles my own experiences of tabletop gaming and ENM, I wouldn't draw any firm conclusions about the wider population from it. But if you've ever wanted an app to help you find a D&D party? It turns out you could do a lot worse than Feeld.

title: MTG Alchemy's new Build-A-Planeswalker card shows the dying format at its best
content:
MTG Arena's Alchemy format may be in its death throes, but with a last strangled gasp it just disgorged one of its wildest designs yet, and I'm tempted to give the online-only game mode another go, just to see this card in action.

That card is Enter the Eternities, a Simic sorcery spell that, for two mana, turns any creature into a randomized planeswalker. Essentially, you're awakening the spark in a creature, turning them into your very own procedurally generated MTG planeswalker card. You're not limited to legendary creatures either. You could have a Colossal Dreadmaw planeswalker, or an Ornithopter, though the latter would die instantly, as it comes in with loyalty equal to its power.

This will presumably work like other cards that have you 'draft' random cards from a spellbook. Essentially three random abilities will be chosen from a possible selection and be scrambled together to create a (possibly) fair and balanced planeswalker.

We don't know what those abilities will be just yet, but players are already pointing out that this has the potential to be surprisingly strong. There's no shortage of undercosted creatures that come in with some sort of drawback, after all, and here you only care about them for their statline.

T1: Slumbering Trudge, T2: Enter the Eternities doesn't sound bad, and with The Ancient One you could even trigger a planeswalker ultimate on turn three. We'll have to see how gamebreaking that can be.

That does it, I'm going to count my wildcards and see if I can afford to spend them on this goofy experiment. It helps that this is a mythic - I always seem to have some of the orange-y bronze wildcards to spare.

Alchemy Reality Fracture, the final Alchemy set ever, comes out next week on October 13, 2026. After that, while the Alchemy cards will still exist and be playable in formats like Historic and Brawl, there won't be any new ones getting made.

title: D&D staff call for fair wages, AI protection, and creative freedom in new Wizards of the Coast union bid
content:
Dungeons and Dragons staff are asking Wizards of the Coast to recognize an official union, it was revealed on October 6. Alongside MTG's Studio X team, D&D's workers intend to join United Wizards of the Coast (UWOTC-CWA), a union formed by MTG Arena staff with Communication Workers of America.

MTG Arena's staff successfully voted to unionize back in June. They too asked Wizards of the Coast and parent company Hasbro to recognize United Wizards of the Coast. However, the unionization was still decided by formal election.

United Wizards of the Coast is now asking for recognition again through a petition. "We are asking Wizards of the Coast and Hasbro management to voluntarily recognize our union by 5:00 p.m. PT on Tuesday, October 13th", it states.

To tabletop fans, the union says "You can encourage our management by signing this petition and sharing our campaign with your communities." "Support from the Magic community was key to MTG Arena's union win, and we hope to capture that same support for our union efforts."

The announcement was met with overwhelming support from Wizards staff on social media. WotC producer Vanessa Hoskins says on Bluesky: "It is another step towards strengthening the gaming industry, and empowering the creatives who make the games you love".

Senior D&D game designer Joey Haeck also shared the petition on Bluesky. "I'm the proudest to be a Wizard I've ever been", they say, adding "this union is the first step to making D&D better than ever before." Principal game designer James Wyatt also says "this has been a long, long time coming!"

Why do Wizards staff want to unionize? In their own words: "We are the stewards of the games that we make, and we deserve to be treated with all the respect and dignity that entails".

The petition calls for "fair wages, career progression, and job security". "Workers should be secure in the face of industry instability, roles should be clearly defined, and workers should be able to grow their careers through meaningful raises, role changes, and promotions."

Like the MTG Arena staff who originally formed United Wizards of the Coast, they also call for remote work protections, sustainable workloads, and "protection against the encroachment of AI". "Leadership, without regard for the desires of our teams, has pushed for adoption of LLMs and generative AI", the union claims. "This has to stop; our teams deserve a robust and enforceable AI policy that aligns with our goals and values."

The union also asks for reliable, accessible healthcare, as well as "full ownership of what we create outside of work". Reportedly, Wizards of the Coast can "currently claim ownership over any IP created by employees during their tenure at Wizards, including works that are fully unrelated to Wizards IP". "What we make in our free time should belong to us, not the company", the union says.

Wargamer has reached out to Wizards of the Coast for comment on the union's petition. We will update this story if we receive a response.

title: HTPE Hobby Diary: Building and Painting His Majesty King Brodd, Part 1
content:
Welcome, my friends, to something a little different. In this miniseries, I’m going to talk you through building and painting a Mega-Gargant - in this case, his regal majesty, King Brodd. This isn’t going to be what you might consider a “normal” How To Paint Everything entry; instead, it’ll be a sort of mashup of Hobby Diary and HTPE with a lot of progress photos.

Loading...

I began by assembling Brodd’s legs and trunk as you’d expect, following the instructions, until I arrived at the “decorate the body” phase. Since my other Mega-Gargant is a Warstomper, I already have a model with the turtleshell Warstomper belly assembly, so I decided to break with Brodd’s instructions and outfit him with the portcullis, planks, and bells assemblage from the Gatebreaker instead. I honestly think it’s a bit of a shame that they didn’t give Brodd his own special belly-decorations piece with more kingly stuff on it; such a notable character deserves a little ornamentation! Look at the mould lines on this gate, Jesus wept; cleaning those was a special kind of torment, honestly.

Loading...

With the exception of the belly decoration, I assembled the rest of Brodd’s bits and pieces according to the instructions until I got to the arms. Rather than the somewhat awkward cross-body Greathammer hold, I wanted Brodd to use the hammer more like a walking staff, since he’s an old fella, after all. To get this to work, I carefully shaved down the part of the hand that fits into the wrist, before packing out the wrist with some very old Miliput. After it had dried a little but was still soft, I jammed the wrist peg into the gap to make a nice impression before letting it dry and cure all the way. The Miliput is essential for this, as otherwise the contact area isn’t large enough and the hammer-holding hand won’t be able to glue into the wrist securely. For the right hand, I chose the hand holding the two humans in various states of distress from the Gatebreaker build.

I made sure the various arms fit nicely to the torso but didn’t glue them in for the sake of making painting a little more straightforward. 

Tip: Miliput, unlike green stuff, is actually water-soluble, meaning you can both smooth it with a wet finger, and dilute it into a very flow-y gap-filling solution that works really well!

Loading...

Onto building the base, I honestly went back and forth on this a few times  - did I want something simple and straightforward, or build a more scenic base with a stronger sense of “being there in the environment I had in my imagination”? Both options have much to recommend them. A simpler base with only texture and grass tufts would be very quick to build and paint, while a scenic base with handmade decorative elements has the potential to be more spectacular, but is much more work and equally has the potential to look bad instead. In the end, I plumped for a scenic base out of a kind of foolhardy masochism. I started by putting down a bunch of Vallejo Diorama Effects Dark Earth; while that was still wet, I started putting together the wooden parts of my scene. The vision I had was that Brodd and his followers were launching a raid on a village, looking for something to loot. Brodd has kicked over the palisade and is stepping through the breach. It stops short of being a “diorama” because it’s really just the one model and I don’t want the base to distract too much from the model itself. Honestly, it’s a shame that the Mega-Gargant kit doesn’t have a piece like the iconic fleeing villager from the WHFB Giants kit! I feel like it would add a lot to the scene to have some little guys running away. Maybe if I feel like it, I can “borrow” the fleeing villager from one of the “little” giants I have knocking about. 

To create the stakes of the palisade, I cut up some dowels to the appropriate length and sharpened them by whittling with a knife. I scratched some bark-like patterns in the side with a very sharp knife (be very very careful if you’re going to try this, the chances of slipping and cutting yourself are very high, if you have a scribing tool, that would almost certainly work better, but I don’t) They’re a bit too regular and smooth to look like real stakes cut from actual trees, but they serve their purpose well enough. 

Loading...

Tip: When making a scenic base, keep checking as you go that your model will actually fit. For models without much ground-clearance, avoid putting scenic elements in the middle of your base (unless your model is going to stand directly on them, straddling a piece of scenery looks weird. It can be helpful to draw an outline around your model’s feet as a guide.

Loading...

When it came to painting, I primed black as normal. I knew I was going to follow my normal method and deal with the most prominent colour first, which in this case is the skin, so I opened with a white airbrush highlight using Molotow One4All White. This approach is a bit different to a zenithal highlight; although the method is similar, it’s not a 1-to-1 comparison. In this case, rather than spraying the entire model from directly above, I carefully highlighted the individual volumes, focusing on places like the thigh and the top of the belly, and building up the colour slowly to avoid flooding the model and making a mess.

One of the chief problems when painting skin over a black-white zenithal highlight is what my friend Juan Hidalgo calls the “blue shift” effect, whereby the lack of warmth in the shadow causes the skin to look lifeless and dead. To avoid this, I sprayed all the shadows with Vallejo Game Color Dark Skin until they were nicely warm. You can also spray an orange-y brown contrast or speedpaint (like Crusader Skin) to achieve a similarly effective undercoat.

Following on from the Dark Skin, I sprayed everywhere except the deepest shadows with Vallejo Game Color Athena Skin, which is a perfect ruddy skin that I use on so many things for that warmth and pinkness. I have a big fondness for the Game Color skin tones, they’re relatively diverse and compartmentalised into 4-part sequences which makes it pretty easy to work up skin without too much guessing.

With the Athena Skin layered almost everywhere, I moved onto the next colour on the ladder, spraying the upward-facing areas with Vallejo Game Color Rosy Flesh, this pink shade won’t be my final tone, but it works as a bridge between the Athena Skin and the main tone for the skin, which is the helpfully named Vallejo Game Color Skin Tone, which I sprayed carefully inside the areas of Rosy Flesh.

For the final colour of this basic skin work-up, I went back to the rosy skin set and used Vallejo Game Color Pale Flesh to spray very fine highlights on the highest parts of the model, taking care to stay inside the areas of Skin Tone as I went. It’s important to stay inside the previous highlights; otherwise, the jump in value will be too great, and the result will look odd.

To add a little pinkness and shading, I used Pro Acryl 1Step Shadow Flesh straight through the airbrush to paint shadows and add some lividity to the skin, on the downward-facing parts of the knees, the undersides of the feet, underneath his boobs, the armpits, the bottom of the belly, the ankles, and parts of the thigh being shaded by the skirt.

Tip: Most hobby paints are far too thick to go through an airbrush as-is, so they need some kind of thinning. For each of these Vallejo Game Color paints, I thin them with some airbrush thinner (Ionic Airbrush Thinner, in this case) and water in a waxed-paper cup - the kind you’d get ketchup in at a fast-food restaurant. Since the cups are only paper, it’s easy to form them into a spout to pour the paint into your airbrush cup. I’ve found that thinning the paints down outside the airbrush has reduced the number of clogs I get by something like 85% and makes airbrushing easier. Note: you don’t need to do this with paints that are already thin, like Pro Acryl 1-Step or Army Painter Speedpaints.

So that’s the first part of painting King Brodd; we’ve got a nice strong foundation upon which to build the rest of this work. Join me next time when I paint the rest of the owl!

title: BattleTech Mech Overview: Venom
content:
This week in BattleTech we're taking a look at the Venom, also known as the fat Spider. It's a side-grade to the Spider, created during the Clan Invasion as an alternative because of high need (because apparently scaling up to make an entirely different mech that uses more advanced technology was the safer choice in case fighting slowed down than just making more spiders? IDK some of that old fluff is wonky). It looks nearly identical, with a set of winglets on the back being the easiest way to visually differentiate it from the Spider, and carries twice the armament while moving just as fast.

Like a Spider, the venom is very good at breaking any sort of mission that involves looting things, with an 8/12/8 movement profile, two hands, and few enough guns that it's generally relatively cheap. While there may be other mechs that are better in specific situations, both the Venom and Spider are safe choices that you can happily put into any list knowing they'll be able to contribute.

It's so similar to the spider that the recognition code stays the same, both 'mechs being SDR-xxx.

Simonson's Cutthroats Venom. Credit: Jack Hunter

Chassis

At 35 tons the Venom is 5 tons heavier than its spider progenitor. Across all variants it makes use of an XL engine to maintain the same 8/12/8 movement profile despite the increased weight, and uses ferro-fibrous armor to give it at least slightly more protection. It's not an omni, so we do see a couple changes across the variants, but the movement profile does remain the same.

Variants

These mechs have all been reviewed based on a standard F through S scale, which you can find described on our landing page here (along with all of our other ‘mech reviews, the name of the box you can buy to get any of the mechs we have covered, and our general methodology).

Venom. Credit: Rockfish

SDR-9K

Venoms start out, like a Spider, with very marginal armor. 62 points is technically more armor than a Spider (which usually have about 53), but can't be described as anywhere near enough for comfort. Every front location has enough that an IS medium pulse won't go internal, and the torsos can take a clan medium pulse, but that's it. Six leg armor and eight leg structure, or seven torso armor and eight side torso structure are exactly not enough to be able to withstand a 15 damage hit. A just over 50% chance to have the mech rendered nonfunctional by a single solid hit is high enough that I'd need this mech to be less than 798 BV for me to be truly happy with it. It's well armed for the mobility with four medium pulses, but that is too many - 12 single heat sinks means it goes up by six heat at a run.

Jack's Rating: C-

SDR-9KA

This first variant trades one medium pulse (bringing it down to three) for 36 more pips of armor (bringing it up to 98 points). It's not a meaningful decrease in firepower, as it couldn't actually fire the fourth pulse without significantly overheating anyways. With at least 10 points of armor everywhere now it can actually take a couple hits without instantly evaporating. It goes up to 865 BV, and I'll happily pay that to have a functioning mech.

Jack's Rating: B

SDR-9KB

Learning the right lessons but doing them wrong, this variant also has three medium pulses and more armor than the stock variant. Instead of being happy with that, it doesn't have quite as much armor, so a 10-damage hit will go internal on the limbs. Two jump jets are dropped, giving it an 8/12/6 move profile. In exchange for those losses, it gets one extra heat sink, so it's neutral walking (yay..............) and...............a machine gun. Yay. Do not spend 769 BV on this.

Jack's Rating: D

Mercenary Venom. Credit: Jack Hunter

SDR-9KC

The third time is definitely the charm for upgrading the stock Venom. For the third time it has three pulses, but this time instead of making bad trades it has an endo-steel internal structure and switches to double heat sinks. It retains the full 8/12/8 move profile and is up to 119 points of armor - it can take a 15 point hit to the legs or CT without it going internal, and with at least 5 points of armor across each rear torso location it can get tapped by a medium laser without too much concern. It does have c3 if you happen to be using that, but even if you aren't it's a solid alternative to a Spider 9M. Same damage potential (if slightly less accurate), better heat management, and significantly more armor; though that all comes out to a relatively expensive 939 BV. Very good, but not quite great - I'd still use the spider whenever possible.

Jack's Rating: A-

SDR-9KE

Skipping over -9KD (maybe that variant code got left unused for another upgraded normal variant down the line), the -9KE gets extremely weird. We're back down to low armor coverage, this time at 80 points. Enough that a 15-point hit won't actually remove a location that matters, but not enough to actually be survivable. A partial wing brings the move profile up to 8/12/10, which is great and very useful, but then filling out the rest of the mech is an ER medium laser, ER flamer, TAG, bloodhound active probe, remote sensor dispenser, and four vehicular mine dispensers. The mine dispensers give you eight turns of dropping 10-point minefields at the beginning or end of your movement, which is vaguely helpful (I think in practice they aren't really strong enough to stop anyone from moving through a hex, and you can't mine multiple hexes in a row without sacrificing your TMM), and the remote sensors give you a really really bad way to spot for indirect LRM fire. The mech has TAG, just use that with semi-guided. This is definitely a mech that exists, and being able to jump 10 with hands and a probe does have utility, but it's definitely not worth 803 BV.

Jack's Rating: D

Final Thoughts

The Spider 9M makes evaluating the Venom hard, because they're essentially the same mech and nothing quite hits the same intersection of cheap, mobile, damaging, and useful that it does. The 9KC variant comes close if you want to pay more for a bit more durability, but you do lose accuracy on the lasers as well as it costing half again as much, so I can't say that it's a good option. Still, if you're stuck in a situation where you already have the Spider and can't bring a second, the 9KC is a good choice.

title: Games from the Crypt #24 - Return of the Vampire
content:
It's time to go back into the Games Crypt once more this fine October for another deadly Halloween delight. And this time it's another freshly exhumed reprint coming to us courtesy Renegade Game Studios, who have a new edition of 2010's Dungeons & Dragons: Castle Ravenloft coming up in February 2027. I was a little surprised to see this one make a comeback not only because it was a fairly extensive production with tons of minis (crappy, but still), dungeon tiles, cards, and the fact that there several other games in this particular D&D product line that were quite a bit more compelling than this one was- regardless of the fact that the gothic horror setting of Ravenloft is my all-time favorite D&D realm.

But let's look back to 2010, when this game first hit. It made quite an impact at the time, and in retrospect I think it was mainly because at the time the only real and current competition on the market for an old school dungeon-crawl board game was Fantasy Fiight's Descent: Journeys in the Dark. But this was a D&D branded, borderline mass-market design that was reasonably priced, self-contained, and ultra simple despite being on the very much not ultra simple 4th edition D&D rule set. It had that X factor charm, that sense that this is a game that kids will buy and play with their friends in their parents' basements or around a kitchen table. More hardcore gamers decried its very basic, simple rules and whiff of a campaign structure and leveling mechanics. But the beer and pretzels crowd glommed right on to what this game was selling.

At the time, I was very much one of its defenders - I thought it captured all the most important elements of a D&D-themed dungeon romp. Hero classes, traps, treasure, monsters galore, and D20 based combat that was fun and quick. The monsters ran on a very basic system that described tactics in an if-than triaging scheme so no DM was required, which distinguished it from its most notable antecedent, HeroQuest and its contemporary Descent. The game was even worth playing solitaire, at a time when solo gaming was really kind of starting to emerge as a significant concern. It was pitched somewhere between Gygax's original Dungeon! board game and the more scenario-based play of subsequent dungeon crawlers. There was text to read to get you into the Ravenloft vibe and the miniature bats, werewolves, hags, and ghosts (despite being crappy as noted) gave it a "box of toys" feel. I'm sure many copies of this game were sold simply to jump-start DM miniature collections.

This was one of those games that everybody was playing for a minute back in 2010, but I found that it was actually maybe a bit too stripped down. The Ravenloft atmosphere wasn't particularly strong with generic dungeon tiles, even when going face to face with Strahd himself in an epic showdown. These days this sense of something missing would mean that an expansion would inevitably trundle onto the market to add things to the chassis. But not so with the line of SKUs that Castle Ravenloft sired. Instead, they made more games based on the core system.

And frankly speaking, all of them were better and the design team refined and iterated on the core mechanics effectively. They all added more narrative, better progression, and up to a point better miniatures (before they completely fell off a cliff in that regard). At one time I had like five or six of these massive titles in their massive boxes, with Wrath of Ashardalon remaining to my mind the standout, offering the best of what these games had to offer.

Looking over Renegade's announcement and online materials for the Castle Ravenloft reprint I have to say that it is somewhat disappointing that the upcoming release is really just kind of a visual assets update with a price tag that is literally twice what it was back in the day. Sure, even at $100 there's a lot in the box - but there's also some 16 years worth of similar games out now that offer more for less.

Regardless of my criticism, I still have a fondness for this game. It's still a solid, appealing dungeoncrawl that you can play with virtually anyone and complete a scenario in an hour. Kids tend to love it and get really into it, which is always a huge positive in my book. And it's always great to see more Ravenloft on shelves, especially at Halloween - except that it's really more of a Valentine's release this time, isn't it?

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

title: Wizards of the Coast Releases Exodus TTRPG, Tying Into Upcoming Sci-Fi Video Game
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Designed by James Ohlen—the veteran RPG designer behind Baldur’s Gate 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic—the game adapts the 5E system for sci-fi play, with new classes, weapons, and factions. The Traveler’s Handbook introduces eight origins, four classes with two subclasses each, and six powerful Traveler Dynasties that serve as in-game factions. The Exodus Encyclopedia packs in stat blocks for constructs, Celestials, changelings, awakened beings, and human NPCs, along with Remnant items for research and combat.

Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.

The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana releases October 28—just in time to send a shiver down your spine before Halloween.

title: CMON Faces Make-or-Break Moment as It Warns of “Prolonged Structural Downturn”
content:
CMON has issued a stark warning about its future, telling investors its core business is stuck in a “prolonged structural downturn” and still burning through more cash than it brings in. The tabletop crowdfunding giant is now racing to raise up to $17.5m from outside investors.

The warning landed alongside CMON’s H1 financial report, and it caps off a brutal 18 months for one of the biggest names in crowdfunded board games.

Parts of this article is based on info from BoardGameWire.

A Company Half Its Former Size

CMON has spent the past year and a half trying to stop the bleeding. The publisher has:

  • Cut its workforce in half
  • Sold off major IP including Zombicide, Blood Rage, and Cthulhu: Death May Die
  • Shut down its Singapore office
  • Halted new crowdfunding campaigns

Those moves have helped — but not enough to fix the underlying problem.

Losses Shrinking, But Cash Still Draining

The good news: CMON’s losses are shrinking fast.

The company posted a loss of just over $2m in the first half of 2026, compared to nearly $7m during the same stretch last year. Revenue also crept up more than 7% year-on-year, hitting $3.68m. Selling and distribution costs were cut by more than half, and administrative expenses dropped from $4.37m to $2.37m.

The bad news: it’s still not enough to keep the lights on without outside help.

CMON’s cash reserves have been in freefall. They sat at $3.9m at the end of 2022, fell to $2.1m by the end of 2024, and slipped to just over $900,000 by June 2025. In early August, the company revealed it had roughly $368,000 on hand — less than a month’s worth of operating expenses.

The Backer Problem: $14m in Undelivered Games

A huge chunk of CMON’s financial pressure comes down to games that backers have already paid for but haven’t received.

Eight crowdfunded titles remain undelivered, representing $14m raised from backers. The two biggest are **DC Super Heroes United** (over $4.4m raised) and DCeased (over $2.5m). Both were originally due last year, but have been delayed repeatedly and are now slated for Q1 2027.

CMON hasn’t completed fulfillment on a crowdfunding project since Zombicide: White Death in mid-2025. It has managed to ship some pre-orders — Cthulhu: Dark Providence, Marvel United: Witching Hour, and Dune: Desert War all went out in the first half of this year — but four more pre-order titles remain in limbo, including the Assassin’s Creed Role Playing Game.

The $17.5m Gamble

To stay afloat, CMON is leaning on a massive rights issue designed to raise up to HK$150.5m (about $19m). The plan lets existing shareholders buy three new shares for every one they already own.

There’s just one problem: shareholders barely took the bait. Only 7.76% of the new shares were claimed by the August deadline, leaving CMON scrambling to find more than $17.5m from other investors — a figure approaching 2.5-times the company’s entire valuation from its last share sale in February.

If the money comes through, here’s how CMON plans to spend it:

  • 40% — Day-to-day operations for roughly a year, including staff, royalties, shipping, and distribution
  • 20% — Paying down debts, including $2.46m owed to a company director and $385,000 in unsecured employee advances
  • 25% — Expansion into existing and new markets, with a focus on Europe, Japan, and the Philippines
  • 15% — Potential acquisitions in digital gaming

The final result of the rights issue is due September 15.

A Digital Pivot — With a Catch

That 15% digital acquisition budget is notable, especially since CMON just walked away from a planned $2.1m investment in NFT game maker Blissful Link. That deal would have valued Blissful Link at over $95m — despite the company posting a loss of about $197,000 in 2024 on revenues of just over $408,000.

CMON says it’s now hunting for one to three businesses, mostly in Asia-Pacific, valued between $1.3m and $2.5m each, to help build digital adaptations and companion apps. The publisher insists physical tabletop games remain its core business and that digital is meant to complement, not replace, them.

Where the Money Comes From Now

The report also lays bare just how dramatically CMON’s geographic revenue has shifted.

North America generated over $8.6m in the first half of 2021 — 57% of the company’s roughly $15.1m revenue at the time. By the first half of 2026, North and South America combined brought in just $642,000.

Europe has collapsed similarly, falling from about $4.5m to $982,000 over the same period.

Asia is now CMON’s largest market by a wide margin, generating over $2m and accounting for about 55% of total revenue — up from less than 10% in 2021. That’s not because Asia is growing, though. Revenue there is down roughly 37% since 2022. It’s just fallen far less than everywhere else.

What’s Next for Crowdfunding?

CMON said back in March that it intended to resume crowdfunding in the second half of 2026. Its latest report doesn’t repeat that promise. Instead, the company says new titles will be developed and launched “selectively” based on market conditions, available cash, and project readiness.

For a publisher built on the crowdfunding model, that’s a notable shift in tone — and a sign that CMON’s road back to stability is still a long one.
